inline.s: As for the method of contemplation: after the Tang dynasty, apart from the Chan school, the schools that expounded it grew fewer and fewer. The Tiantai school, for instance, when lecturing on the teachings, set forth the principles of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle in considerable detail; yet in actual practice it did not necessarily use this method. Only the Chan school, from ancient times, spoke of the one step above, and would not allow the mind, intellect, or consciousness to be used in investigation. Hence arose the saying that the other Dharma gates still employ thought, and only Chan does not. This was supported by citing the scripture that one may not take the mind of birth and death as the cause of one's cultivation. Such people do not understand that the prohibition against using mind, intellect, and consciousness in investigation means only that ordinary deluded feeling must not be used to conjecture; for the moment consciousness is used, that is ordinary feeling. To conjecture the Buddha's teaching with the feelings of an ordinary person can never be right; therefore it is forbidden. The ancients also said that contemplation is illumination, and illumination is dwelling in illumination. Later generations criticized this, holding that such dwelling in illumination is dark realization. Since ordinary conjecture is forbidden, and illumination is dark realization, while the original meaning of contemplation is thought and investigation, students were left with nowhere to turn.

How, then, should one actually begin the practice of contemplation? This humble man investigated the matter for many years, and from Master Nanyue's Mahayana Calm and Insight grasped its principle. When the ancients said that mind, intellect, and consciousness may not be used in investigation, they meant that the mind of birth and death may not be taken as the cause of one's cultivation. The Buddha's intent was in fact not so. That saying means that when one who studies the Buddha Dharma first arouses the mind, he may not take the mind of birth and death as the cause of his cultivation. This is the meaning of this sutra's 'good men and good women who arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.' As for actual practice, thought must be employed. Thus this sutra says, 'All the various kinds of living beings, I shall cause them all to enter nirvana without residue and be brought to deliverance' — this is thought. To arouse the supreme bodhi mind at the outset is to cultivate from the basis of the nature: this is what is meant by not taking the mind of birth and death as the cause of one's cultivation. As for practice, it must employ contemplation and illumination, and that is thought. The Chan school's saying that mind, intellect, and consciousness may not be used in investigation is the patriarchs' painstaking concern; in reality thought is still required, for without thought the doubt-sensation cannot arise. As for not conjecturing with ordinary feeling, that is another matter again. How do we know that after the Tang the other schools mostly did not understand how to contemplate? This can be proved by Master Shandao's explanation in his commentary on the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations. He says: 'People today have dull faculties, and their contemplation does not succeed, and so I advocate only Buddha-recitation.' This refers to the vastness of the contemplation method of the Contemplation Sutra, to which the measure of an ordinary mind cannot correspond. But one must not, because Master Shandao said this, set the contemplation method aside and never speak of it. After the middle of the Tang dynasty the Esoteric school flourished exceedingly for a time, and before long was extinguished. The Huayan school fared likewise, and the Tiantai school also declined midway. Through the advocacy of the two masters Siming and Ciyun, and with the various sutra commentaries recovered from Japan, it was able to revive. Yet the actual practice of these two masters was also Pure Land recitation, not calm and insight. After the Song, the Pure Land school still had several masters, but the method of contemplation was likewise mostly not discussed. Thus only the Chan school still preserved the gate of contemplation. Practitioners of later ages were by no means few, yet those who gained power were few; this has a good deal to do with the neglect of the method of contemplation.

Again, practitioners often find the first stages of practice very effective, and afterward change. This too comes of not knowing how to contemplate: the practice grows dry and flavorless, and so it goes. Others read and recite the Mahayana scriptures and can understand their principle, yet in the end give rise to wrong views — this also is because they do not know how to contemplate. Others again read and recite the scriptures in great quantity, yet the principle remains a principle, having nothing to do with body and mind; greed, anger, and delusion do not diminish in the least — this too is because they do not know how to contemplate. Contemplation is thought. Illumination has two meanings: one is dwelling in illumination, the other is seeing through illumination. Seeing through illumination refers to the time when the work has been accomplished in cultivation, as in the Heart Sutra's 'seeing through illumination that the five aggregates are all empty.' Broadly speaking, seeing through illumination comes from dwelling in illumination, and dwelling in illumination comes from thought. Without thought one cannot dwell in illumination; without dwelling in illumination one cannot see through illumination. When thought continues long, the mind comes to rest in one place, and that is dwelling in illumination. At that time many idle thoughts stop for a while and no longer come to disturb; if they come to disturb, one cannot abide. Every person's present single thought possesses the true mind inherently; only because idle thoughts disturb it does one fail to awaken. Once idle thoughts stop, the originally inherent light naturally reveals itself, and this is wisdom. Contemplation and illumination must contemplate our own mind-nature; this is what is called dissolving back into the self-nature. Yet ordinary people cannot reach it by contemplation: they are wholly a black lacquer barrel, wholly the deluded mind — what is to be done? There is nothing for it but to contemplate according to the Buddha's teaching, that is, to work first with the words of the Buddhist scriptures. The Buddha's teaching of the method of contemplation and illumination is precisely that we may not conjecture with ordinary feeling. Take this passage of scripture: if one conjectures it with ordinary feeling and does not contemplate, one cannot understand it. People of the world who read the sutras seek only in the words and think they have understood the meaning — this is utterly impermissible. Take the line 'they should thus subdue their minds': conjecture it with ordinary feeling, and of course there will be many interpretations; these must not be accepted and should be dismissed. Then think again, and other sorts of states appear, and these too must be dismissed. Thinking and thinking again, all must be dismissed. The more one thinks and the further one goes, the more one becomes like an idiot — and the wonder lies precisely in this word 'idiot.' The ancients said: one must die a great death. To die means to die to this deluded mind. Working in this way, whether for half a year or a year, one suddenly opens to enlightenment, beyond all expectation. One must then seek a good friend in the Dharma to verify whether it accords. If there is no good friend, then let the Buddhist scriptures be the proof. If the scriptures contain no such teaching, it is still ordinary conjecture. In this way many idle thoughts in the mind are cut off. Though this is not yet dissolving back into the self-nature, a great deal has already been dissolved. Therefore one must read and recite the Mahayana scriptures a great deal. This sutra everywhere speaks of reading, reciting, receiving, and upholding; receiving and upholding is contemplation and illumination.

Next, contemplate 'all the various kinds of living beings ... and in truth not one being attains deliverance.' The preceding text spoke of subduing; why does this passage not mention subduing? What does it mean? This is to cause us to expand the measure of our minds to the utmost, to the boundless and limitless great. For the great root of the sickness of living beings is that the measure of their minds is narrow and small; being narrow and small, they cling to a self. Therefore the Buddha has us enlarge this mind, transforming it imperceptibly — what is called 'the great transforming it.' If in the ordinary affairs of daily use one constantly contemplates and illuminates in this way, taking the Buddha's enlargement of the mind's measure and applying it to one's own part, this is the wondrous method for ridding oneself of the view of self and removing affliction.

Next, contemplate this passage of scripture: its conclusion rests in the single line 'in truth not one being attains deliverance.' This is to cause us to rid ourselves of the view of self, and yet it does not point directly at the view of self; instead it takes the side of the beings who stand opposite and contemplates there. For ordinary people cling to a self and will not let go for a single moment. If one contemplates with regard to the self, one cannot gain power; therefore one contemplates from the side of living beings, contemplating that causes and conditions gather and that the very substance is empty. And again, living beings share one substance. Contemplating and illuminating in this way, imperceptibly the clinging to self is naturally dissolved. This is the skillful and subtle method of dissolving back into the self-nature. Next, contemplate 'whether born from eggs' and on to 'neither percipient nor non-percipient.' It can be seen that all living beings alike possess desire, form, and consciousness. If these three are not shifted, one forever revolves within the three realms. Hence we know that desire must be cut off, that form must not be clung to, and that consciousness must be shifted. Contemplating and illuminating in this way, imperceptibly desire, form, and consciousness can be removed.

Next, contemplate 'I shall cause them all to enter nirvana without residue and be brought to deliverance.' Since living beings are as numerous as this — the egg-born so stupid, the fixed-nature so hard to transform, the percipient and non-percipient so arrogant — how can they all be brought to deliverance? Yet the Buddha's is an unconditional great compassion: whoever comes near him, he will surely deliver. Contemplating and illuminating in this way, one is ashamed to be merely human: above, one has not yet cultivated to the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception; below, one is loftier than the egg-born and moisture-born. One ought to learn from the Buddha and become a Buddha; the supreme mind naturally arises, and the deluded mind naturally turns.

Next, contemplate the single line 'in truth not one being attains deliverance,' placed beneath the line 'living beings without measure, without number, without bound.' It can be seen that if there is one being undelivered, my vow is not yet exhausted. Contemplating the Buddha's words in this way, principle does not separate from fact and fact does not separate from principle; this is the mutual fusion of principle and fact. 'I shall cause them all to enter nirvana without residue and be brought to deliverance' dismisses clinging to emptiness; 'in truth not one being attains deliverance' dismisses clinging to existence. Both sides are dismissed: this is the double negation. Both sides are likewise practiced: this is the double illumination. This is negation and illumination at the same time. Such contemplation can realize the fruit of stillness and illumination at the same time. That all living beings are brought to deliverance is great compassion; that in truth not one being attains deliverance is great wisdom. This is the mutual fusion of compassion and wisdom, by which one attains the Buddha-fruit of dwelling neither in birth and death nor in nirvana. 'I shall cause them all to enter nirvana without residue and be brought to deliverance' is the cultivation of merit; 'in truth not one being attains deliverance' is the cultivation of wisdom. This is the double cultivation of merit and wisdom, by which one realizes the fruit of the One Honored and Two-Footed.

The two words 'diamond' and 'cutter' mean the severing of delusion. Delusion is nothing but views and thoughts, and views and thoughts are precisely the mark of self. This sutra severs the mark of self, and therein lies its tremendous function. To dissolve the view of self is to turn the seventh consciousness into the wisdom of equality. To cause them all to enter nirvana without residue and be brought to deliverance, without giving rise to discrimination, is to turn the sixth consciousness into the wisdom of wonderful observation. That in truth not one being attains deliverance is to turn the eighth consciousness into the great perfect mirror wisdom. Hence the later words: 'all Buddhas and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra.' Is not Buddhahood, then, right here in this one passage of scripture!

All the Mahayana scriptures say that one who arouses the Mahayana mind, not yet having delivered himself, must first deliver others — this is great compassion. Yet in delivering others one is delivering oneself. If one can see this principle clearly through contemplation and illumination, then the Buddha Dharma, though it seems vast and boundless, is in fact intimate and full of flavor; though it seems lofty and profound, it is fundamentally plain and simple. Place this passage of scripture in your mind and constantly contemplate and illuminate it; settle the mind in one place, and idle thoughts gradually dissolve. With just these few lines, there is more than enough for Buddhahood.

Next, contemplate this passage of scripture: not speaking of subduing is itself subduing. It is that we should arouse this vow and make our resolve firm; then clinging to self and the view of self are all swept away, and subduing is contained within — one naturally receives the benefit. Place this passage in your mind every day, and the benefit is inexhaustible; therefore contemplation and illumination are necessary.

blocks.text: Wondrous Practice, Dwelling in Nothing, Section Four

inline.s: (Ren) Second, explaining that not dwelling in marks is precisely right dwelling. Four parts: (Gui) First, directly explaining non-dwelling; second, expounding the reason; third, concluding and showing right dwelling; fourth, further clarifying the why. (Gui) First, again three: (Zi) First, indicating and showing; second, pointing out and explaining; third, concluding.
(Zi) First, indicating and showing.
'Moreover, Subhuti, a bodhisattva should give in such a way as not to dwell in dharmas — that is, in giving.'

'Moreover' means again; 'next' means in sequence. The word 'dharma' embraces all phenomena: every thing and every matter, whether seen by the eye or heard by the ear, or else unseen, unheard, and merely thought of by the mind, is also called a dharma. All worldly dharmas and world-transcending dharmas are included, and so it is called all dharmas. 'Should not dwell' is the direct answer to 'how should one abide?' To dwell means to cling. Living beings cling everywhere: if not to the east, then to the west. The World-Honored One's answer here is precisely a blow straight to the head. Giving is one of the six paramitas, also called the six paramitas. The Great Prajna Sutra enumerates the six paramitas one by one; this sutra speaks only of giving. As to the wording, this avoids the cumbersome and takes the simple; but giving can encompass all dharmas. In the Buddha Dharma one must practice, not dwell. These two lines are as if to say: one should not dwell anywhere, and yet practice all dharmas.

Wherever the two words 'moreover, next' are placed in a sutra, the present text must have a close relation to the preceding text. Here there are two meanings: one is to supplement the previous meaning, the other is to restate the previous meaning. The preceding text answered 'subduing'; this answers 'abiding.' It looks like another meaning, but it is really one and the same matter. For the former speaking of subduing already implies dwelling without dwelling, and this speaking of not dwelling yet dwelling also contains the meaning of subduing; they illumine each other. Moreover, the former aroused the great vow, and this arouses the great practice. Vow and practice cannot be separated: where there is a vow there must be practice, and where there is practice there must be a vow. Nor are they divided into before and after; only when realized in practice is a vow not an empty vow. Hence the close relation. This is the sense in which it supplements the preceding text. Again, the preceding text aroused the great mind to deliver living beings without measure, without number, without bound, but did not speak of the method of delivering them; this precisely speaks of the method of delivering them, and is a further stage of restatement. 'Should not dwell' means not clinging to existence; 'the practice of giving' means again not clinging to emptiness. This is the middle way that does not fall to either side.

The meaning of the six paramitas should be known in rough outline. The six paramitas are giving, precept-keeping, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and prajna. These six are nothing but precept, concentration, and wisdom, counteracting greed, anger, and delusion.

Giving has three kinds: the giving of wealth, the giving of Dharma, and the giving of fearlessness. To give others food, clothing, medicine, and other daily necessities, which requires the use of money, is called the giving of wealth. To expound the sutras and speak the Dharma for others, or to print and present the scriptures, or even worldly books — so long as they benefit people and are used in giving — is called the giving of Dharma. The giving of fearlessness is to rescue others from suffering and hardship. When living beings are in disaster they are sure to be frightened; I go to rescue them and make them fearless. If only I can rescue them, I do not even spare my body and life — this is the giving of fearlessness. Three are one and one is three. For example, to rescue people from hardship and make them fearless is nothing but the giving of wealth and the giving of Dharma. Thus it can be seen that in giving wealth, the giving of Dharma and the giving of fearlessness are also included. Again, to speak the Dharma for others is the wealth of Dharma; to bestow scriptures on others, causing their merit and wisdom to grow, is the giving of fearlessness. Expanded further, there is inner giving and outer giving, and even ultimate giving, as spoken of in the Avatamsaka Sutra, where the categories are extremely many, yet combined they are one. To cultivate giving is to break the grudging and greedy mind. Greed inevitably brings stinginess, and stinginess inevitably brings greed; this can create all kinds of karma and keep one long in the bitter sea of birth and death. Therefore it must be broken.

Precept means the moral discipline. The word 'keeping' differs from the word 'observing': to hold it fast in the bosom, never relaxing for a moment, is to keep. Precepts differ for the householder and the renunciate. For the householder there are the three refuges and the precepts: the five precepts, the bodhisattva precepts, and the samaya precepts of the Esoteric school. For the renunciate there are the three refuges and the precepts: the novice precepts, the bhiksu precepts, and the bodhisattva precepts. Though the five precepts consist only of the five items — no killing, no stealing, no sexual misconduct, no lying, no intoxicants — they are the root of all precepts. Even the renunciate precepts are based on these five, only analyzed in special detail. The renunciate bodhisattva precepts are the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts, laid down by the Buddha for those who leave home. Householders are also permitted to receive them, but must examine themselves and be able to bear them before doing so. Otherwise the Buddha has bodhisattva precepts laid down for laymen and laywomen, somewhat simpler than those for renunciates: six major and twenty-eight minor precepts. Householders would therefore do well to receive these.

Keeping the precepts is the foundation of studying the Buddha Dharma, and is of the utmost importance. It is like building a house: one must first make the foundation firm, or it will surely collapse. Hence this sutra says that those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit can give rise to faith in these chapter-and-verse passages and take them as true. It can be seen that the whole Buddha Dharma is built upon the precepts. Though the precepts are many, they fall into two gates: one is 'ceasing and keeping,' the other is 'doing and keeping.' Ceasing and keeping works on the negative side; doing and keeping works on the positive side. Ceasing and keeping is 'do no evil'; doing and keeping is 'practice all good.' These two phrases have been worn threadbare in the world, but they in fact come from the Buddhist scriptures. The student first keeps on the side of ceasing, then advances to keeping on the side of doing. Not to kill is good, but that is only ceasing and keeping; to go further and urge others to abstain from killing is doing and keeping. Not only to abstain from killing but also to release living creatures is still more doing and keeping. Someone may say, 'I can abstain from killing and from stealing' — but is this so easy? To keep the precept against killing, one must not harm even the life of a mosquito or a fly. If some matter was not made clear to others and they think it was I who did it, that is a breach of the precept against stealing. Or in a public office, to use a public envelope or a sheet of official letter paper for private business is also a breach of the precept against stealing. As for the precept against sexual misconduct, the Buddha laid down for householders only abstinence from improper sexual conduct; this too is a skillful means, for in truth lust must be cut off, since it is the root of birth and death. The precept against lying, with the addition of harsh speech, divisive speech, and idle talk, opens into four. To revile with evil words is harsh speech; to stir up right and wrong is divisive speech; to describe the feelings of men and women is idle talk, which men of letters are most prone to commit. When the Buddha first laid down the fundamental great precepts, they were only the four: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying. Afterward, because intoxicants can disorder the nature, he added this precept. The first four are natural precepts; the last is a preventive precept. Hence the precept against intoxicants may sometimes be suspended: if illness requires the use of liquor, the Buddha also permitted it. One who keeps the precepts must understand the principle of suspension and prohibition: where suspension applies there is no prohibition, where prohibition applies there is no suspension; sometimes it is permitted, and when permitted there is no breach. Therefore one must distinguish clearly between suspension and prohibition, or the keeping of precepts cannot be complete. The precepts laid down by the Buddha are stricter than worldly law. Thus one who has received only the preliminary precepts is not permitted to read the precepts above them; to read them is to steal the Dharma. Among renunciates, a novice may not read the bhiksu precepts, and a bhiksu may not read the bodhisattva precepts. For the methods of keeping differ, and so one who has not received them may not read them. As for the reason householders are not permitted to read the renunciate precepts — the renunciate precepts being exceedingly heavy, with two hundred and fifty for a bhiksu and three hundred and eighty-four for a bhiksuni — the reason householders may not read them is the Buddha's painstaking concern lest householders thereby create evil karma. For living beings all share one grave sickness: in censuring others they are detailed, in censuring themselves they are lenient. The bhiksu precepts are truly hard to keep; one breaches them at every turn. The Buddha feared that if laymen read them — not having received them themselves — they would censure renunciates all the more severely. Again, the precepts laid down by the Buddha are not like worldly law, which has only articles: in stating a precept, he would first explain in full the principle and the facts that should be kept, and only then lay down the article. At that time many disciples in the Buddhist order who had already reached a high level still could not avoid breaching the precepts; the Buddha feared that students would think, 'They still breach them, so we may be excused,' and therefore did not permit them to read. Keeping the precepts breaks greed, anger, and delusion alike. To speak of them separately: the precept against killing chiefly counters anger; against stealing, chiefly greed; against sexual misconduct, chiefly greed and delusion; against lying, likewise chiefly greed and delusion; against intoxicants, greed, anger, and delusion. In the beginning one keeps the precepts with weight on the facts; but after receiving the bodhisattva precepts, a single stirring of the mind is a breach.

Patience is also translated as 'peaceful endurance'; patience is one kind of peaceful endurance. 'Patience' here is not to be understood as forbearance, but as accepting in accord. Hence peaceful endurance is accepting with a peaceful mind. When others insult me, that is the hardest thing to endure; if one can endure insult, then there is nothing one cannot endure. Therefore patience is cited to cover the rest. Again, patience is not only with regard to insult: in the Buddhist scriptures there is also patience in regard to dharmas, and the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. For example, when the Buddha speaks the Dharma, if we can carry it out in accordance with it, without the slightest deviation, that is patience in regard to dharmas. Again, the principle that arising is fundamentally non-arising — if we can understand it and carry it out, without the slightest deviation, that is the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. Patience breaks the mind of anger.

Vigor means advancing, and has the two meanings of fine and precise. To advance without blindly following is to be fine; to advance step by step without skipping grades is to be precise. Vigor breaks indolence.

Meditative concentration is a double rendering, Sanskrit and Chinese: the Sanskrit is dhyana, the Chinese is 'concentration.' The double rendering is used so that people may know this is the concentration of the Buddhist gate, not the concentration of other paths. It is like 'repentance,' where 'repent' is the Sanskrit ksama and 'ance' is Chinese: the double rendering shows that Buddhist repentance has all sorts of methods such as prostration, and differs from ordinary regret for wrongdoing. When the mind is settled in one place, after a long time concentration is attained, and the attainment of concentration is called samadhi. Meditative concentration counteracts distraction, torpor, and restlessness.

Prajna is a transliteration, indicating the right wisdom that arises from the substance of the nature; it differs from worldly cleverness and dialectical acuity. Worldly cleverness and dialectical acuity are one of the eight difficulties. Lest it be confused with worldly wisdom, it is not translated as 'wisdom' but kept as prajna. Prajna counteracts stupidity and delusion.

In speaking of the six paramitas, they are in fact precept, concentration, and wisdom; the other three paramitas are auxiliaries to these three trainings. Though six are spoken of, the master is prajna. Therefore if prajna does not arise, the other five paramitas cannot be called paramitas either. Hence the Buddha said the five are the feet and prajna is the eyes. Giving and the rest up to meditative concentration also exist in worldly dharmas. That the Buddha Dharma is so subtle and vast, able to deliver living beings universally from all suffering, to end the two kinds of birth and death, and even to dwell neither in birth and death nor in nirvana, is accomplished by nothing but the right wisdom of prajna. Therefore, if prajna is not clearly understood, one cannot enter the Buddha's gate.

The sutra, among the six paramitas, singles out giving alone, because the six paramitas can encompass the ten thousand practices, and giving can encompass the other five. Besides the giving of wealth, the giving of Dharma can encompass vigor, meditative concentration, and prajna. For the Buddha Dharma most values concentration and wisdom: in cause they are calm and insight, in fruit they are concentration and wisdom. One who speaks the Dharma must have calm and insight and the work of vigor before he can speak for others. The giving of fearlessness, again, can encompass precept-keeping and patience. One who keeps the precepts does no evil and practices all good, never offending others, peacefully enduring and accepting; others do not fear him, and this is the giving of fearlessness.

The ancient worthies, explaining this passage, all say that giving can encompass the six paramitas and the ten thousand practices, and therefore the Buddha spoke only of giving, which encompasses all dharmas. Yet it is also acceptable to say that giving itself is all dharmas. For example, the giving of Dharma makes people know precept-keeping, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and prajna, which are the other five paramitas. The giving of fearlessness makes people understand birth and death and so be fearless; and to understand birth and death one must also practice the other five paramitas. Nor is this all: any one paramita may pervade all the others. Thus precept-keeping must be practiced together with giving and the other five; patience, vigor, and meditative concentration are likewise, and each can encompass all dharmas. Again, if the five paramitas are separated from prajna, none can be brought into practice. It can be seen that prajna is the deepest and highest, and is the root of each paramita. Yet why did the Buddha not single out prajna, but single out giving? The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says: 'The non-arising of all dharmas arises from prajna.' Hence we know that the work of practicing all dharmas, being able not to cling to marks, is precisely prajna; therefore giving had to be singled out. Giving is actual practice; thus it can be seen that one who cultivates the Buddha Dharma must not stop at understanding the principle but must actually practice. Precisely because it is actual practice, only giving can encompass all dharmas. If one does not practice all dharmas, how can one deliver living beings? And one who practices all dharmas while clinging to marks likewise cannot deliver living beings.

That one who has not yet delivered himself must first deliver others is a constant saying of those who study the Mahayana; yet one must first ask whether one truly has the capacity. If one cannot apply oneself earnestly and devotes oneself solely to the work of delivering living beings, one cannot avoid seeking outward. Hence the Great Treatise says: 'If a bodhisattva arouses the mind and at once goes to deliver living beings, there is no such ground.' What then is to be done? It is said: one should first arouse the great mind, and in practicing all dharmas, as to where to begin the practice — one begins with giving. Giving is not only first among the six paramitas, it is also first among the four means of gathering: giving, kind words, beneficial conduct, and cooperation. The Buddha's dressing and eating were everywhere the same as those of living beings, and this is nothing but the four means of gathering. Living beings are by nature stiff and strong and do not easily comply; therefore one must first give them what they need. Then with kind and lovely words one makes them glad to hear. And whatever worldly dharma they wish to practice, one further benefits them in that: as when one who seeks a child obtains a child, or one who seeks wealth obtains wealth. And one works alongside them at their tasks; only then can living beings be gathered and accepted by one. Hence this section, closely following the preceding on delivering living beings, points out the method of beginning.

Moreover, giving is the whole Buddha Dharma. From beginning to end the Buddha Dharma is nothing but the one word 'renounce,' and giving is renunciation. Extending this: precept-keeping renounces greed, anger, and delusion; patience renounces anger; vigor renounces indolence, torpor, and restlessness; meditative concentration renounces distraction and torpor; prajna renounces the two extremes and the clinging to self and to dharmas. The six paramitas are nothing but renunciation. Hence we know that giving is the one that is all, and that in cultivating the Buddha Dharma one carries it through from head to tail, from first to last. In the scripture, after the words 'delivering living beings' it speaks only of giving — truly it goes to the vital point. The Small Vehicle also has the work of practicing renunciation, which is spoken of as practicing and renouncing at once. In this text, beneath the word 'practice' is added the word 'in,' which puts the weight on giving.

The preceding statement that giving is nothing but renunciation was a horizontal account. In fact, whether one learns below and reaches above, or speaks vertically, it is likewise nothing but the one word 'renounce.' For example, one who hears the sutra renounces worldly amusements and comes to study the Buddha Dharma; a god renounces the desire realm and ascends to the form realm, renounces the form realm and ascends to the formless realm; one who renounces clinging to self realizes arhatship; one who renounces clinging to dharmas becomes a bodhisattva; and one who renounces even renunciation becomes a Buddha. Hence, vertically too, giving is a thoroughgoing work.

The Buddha's speaking of the Dharma is a perfect sound, complete on every side. 'Practicing giving' on the surface appears to be not grasping the non-dharma; yet giving is renunciation, which is not grasping dharmas. Therefore, in singling out giving, it means not clinging to either extreme — and this holds for every line of this sutra. Someone may doubt: if one grasps neither dharmas nor non-dharmas, the student is faulted whichever way he turns, so how is he to begin? In fact it is not hard: one must know that when we go to practice giving, we can be free of both extremes. In the act, first not dwelling in emptiness is practicing dharmas. The Buddha said: better to cling to existence as to Mount Sumeru than to cling to nothingness as to a mustard seed; therefore one must first block up the gate of emptiness. To apply the mind wholly to the practice of dharmas and to exert oneself on dharmas is to be free of the mark of annihilation. One need only carry on and, at the same time, not keep it in the mind, and then both extremes are avoided. But to give with an ulterior purpose is to dwell, to cling — it is merely defiled merit. Not only is it not merit; some even fall because of it. The word 'renounce' in today's new vocabulary is 'sacrifice.' If one lives in the world and will sacrifice for society, one can surely be public-minded and forget private interest, devoted to the country and forgetful of family. It can be seen that the one dharma of giving includes everything; therefore the Buddha Dharma should be studied not only by those who leave the world, but even by one who is a human being in the world, who likewise cannot afford not to know it.
(Zi) Second, pointing out and explaining.
'What is called giving without dwelling in form, without dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas.'

'What is called' refers to what has been spoken before. Lest people doubt how on earth one should not dwell while practicing all dharmas, the Buddha tells them: it is just as I have said before — not dwelling in the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and even anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Here, to put it briefly, he cites the six dusts: form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas. The six dusts are the objects in the object, practice, and fruit of cultivation; citing them can encompass all dharmas. All the myriad appearances seen by the eye-faculty are form. What is heard by the ear-faculty is sound. What is smelled by the nose-faculty is fragrance. What is tasted by the tongue-faculty is taste. What is contacted by the body-faculty is touch. The discriminations of the mind-faculty as it stirs and moves: some arise toward form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch, and some arise toward what is not form, not sound, not fragrance, not taste, and not touch. The kinds are exceedingly many, and there is no way to name them, so they are named dharmas. The name 'six dusts' has two meanings. One speaks of their being without measure and without bound, as numerous as fine dust; the other carries a sense of defilement, for the moment we touch them we are defiled. Not to dwell is not to cling; the moment there is clinging, the mind is not pure. Speaking in terms of giving: if one gives with an ulterior purpose, contending for one's own face, one dwells in form. If one wishes others to know of it, one dwells in sound. If one wishes everyone to hear of one's fine name, one dwells in fragrance. If one wishes everyone to praise it with their mouths, one dwells in taste. If one gives for the sake of later reward, one dwells in touch. If one does it with deliberate intent, one dwells in dharmas. Therefore the mind must dwell nowhere at all before it is a paramita. 'Paramita' is used everywhere in the Indian language, just as here we say 'arrived home.'

The preceding words 'a bodhisattva, with regard to dharmas' referred to all dharmas; here the six dusts alone are cited, and in this there is much wondrous meaning. Here one must use contemplation and illumination, contemplating step by step, from outer to inner, from coarse to fine. (1) The Buddha did not speak of all dharmas but only of the six dusts, truly to make us know that all dharmas should not be dwelt in. (2) Why should all dharmas not be dwelt in? One should know that the moment one dwells, one is defiled. (3) The Buddha's citing of the six dusts is profound in principle. Why? To speak of form, there is the eye-faculty; to speak of sound, there is the ear-faculty; and so on to speaking of dharmas, where there is the mind-faculty. Faculty and object stand in opposition, and in citing the six dusts the six faculties are already implied. The shallow see shallowly and merely do not dwell in objects; the deep see deeply and can not dwell in the mind. (4) Faculties are faculties and dusts are dusts — how do they come into relation? The medium between them is the six consciousnesses. If consciousness does not arise, faculty and object do not come into relation; this is what is meant by 'when the mind is not present, one looks and does not see, hears and does not hear, eats and does not know the taste.' The Buddha's intent is that not only should objects not be dwelt in, but consciousness too should not be dwelt in. He would have the student know that the root of the calamity of dwelling in objects lies in consciousness, that is, the discriminating mind, and that one should begin at the point where the mind stirs and moves, not dwelling in consciousness. Step by step in this way, one can dissolve back into the self-nature.

How is one to be attentive when the mind stirs and moves? Speaking in terms of giving, whenever the mind stirs and moves, it does not go beyond three kinds: first, for one's own self; second, thinking that others will repay one's kindness; third, thinking to obtain reward. Giving is nothing but the two givings of wealth and Dharma (the giving of fearlessness being included in the giving of Dharma). Often one first feels that one cannot bear to part with it, and there is already an 'I' present. One must know that wealth and Dharma are nothing but the six dusts, and these must not be dwelt in. Working at the point where the thought arises, one sets the self aside, and then perhaps the clinging to self can be broken. After giving, one hopes others will repay one's kindness. One must know that what repays is nothing but the six dusts, and these must not be dwelt in; set aside the thought of looking for repayment. Having given, one hopes to obtain reward. Reward too is nothing but the six dusts, and must not be dwelt in; set aside the thought of reward. (5) If one contemplates and illuminates repeatedly and yet the view of self remains, what then? One should advance to contemplating the way of the three wheels being empty in substance. In giving there is the giver (what gives), the receiver (what is given to), and the thing given. I now contemplate giver and receiver: their very substance is empty. Why? Because all are produced by causes and conditions. Giver and receiver being empty, the thing given is empty too; this is called the three wheels being empty in substance. If one can work hard at this, breaking the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, then the view of self dissolves of itself and one realizes the self-nature. Someone may ask: if the three aspects of giving are complete, why is it called a wheel? They do not know that this in fact has deep meaning. First, it means traveling: the Buddha's speaking of giving is meant to deliver people, and a wheel has the sense of ferrying across. The practitioner gives at all times and so can grind affliction to bits, and a wheel has the sense of grinding. This speaking of giving without dwelling in form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas is precisely to make us understand the way of the three wheels being empty in substance. The giving of wealth is the six dusts; the giving of Dharma is the dharma-dust — all are dharmas produced by conditions. Knowing already that the very substance is empty, why should one dwell? Having contemplated the three wheels as empty in substance, one of course does not dwell.
(Zi) Third, concluding.
'Subhuti, a bodhisattva should give thus, not dwelling in marks.'

The two words 'thus' refer to the preceding words about giving without dwelling in form and giving without dwelling in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas. 'Not dwelling in marks' is by no means annihilation. Not dwelling is renunciation; yet whether renunciation can be ultimate, without the slightest dwelling, is not easy to speak of. Hence the Avatamsaka distinguishes many kinds of renunciation, and at the last speaks of ultimate renunciation: only when the mind does not cling in the least and does not fall to either extreme is it ultimate. This saying, 'not dwelling in marks,' already includes both extremes: it means dwelling neither in the marks of dharmas nor in the marks of non-dharmas. How do we know that the word 'marks' here can encompass non-marks? It can be proved from the preceding text. 'Should not dwell' is not dwelling in the marks of dharmas; 'practicing giving' is not dwelling in the marks of non-dharmas. 'What is called giving without dwelling in form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas' is not dwelling in existence. 'A bodhisattva should give thus' is not dwelling in emptiness. One must know that not dwelling is not annihilation: not dwelling is precisely practicing. To dwell is to be unable to practice; to practice is to be unable to dwell. One who cultivates the bodhisattva path can certainly not dwell in the six dusts; yet if one annihilates, one cannot deliver living beings, for living beings are dwelling precisely in the realm of the six dusts, and so one should deliver them from just this point.

The preceding text says, 'should not dwell, practicing giving'; the following text at once says, 'should give thus, not dwelling in marks.' The Buddha's meaning is that a bodhisattva should, as I have said, cling to neither extreme and practice the middle way. It can be seen that not dwelling is by no means not practicing, and that not dwelling in marks is no empty talk: the essential thing is that in the midst of actual practice one clings neither to existence nor to emptiness, and only then does one accord. The whole sutra breaks marks, and here it is brought out. The Buddha's meaning is as if to say: I am not teaching you not to dwell in dharmas, but not to dwell in the marks of dharmas.

In cultivation one must of course leave the objects of dust, yet not dwelling in the six dusts is far easier said than done. Therefore the fundamental purport of cultivation is non-dwelling, but at the outset one cannot annihilate objects. Take Buddha-recitation, for example: contemplating the Buddha's image is a form-object; heavenly music and waterfowl are sound-objects; the fragrant purity of the lotus is a fragrance-object; eating and walking are taste-objects; receiving all manner of bliss is a touch-object; mindfulness of Amitabha is a dharma-object. Hence the two words 'not dwelling' must be clearly recognized: they are by no means annihilation. Annihilation is emptiness, which is also non-dharma. Giving encompasses all marks of dharmas and also encompasses the marks of non-dharmas. Therefore 'not dwelling' means not dwelling in dharmas and not dwelling in non-dharmas. People of the world who give up their lives are also renouncing, only they dwell in marks. To be loyal and serve the country, to kill oneself to perfect benevolence, at most makes one a god. If when giving up one's life one harbors a self-seeking mind or a mind of hatred, one may even fall. Young men and women who give up their lives for love likewise easily fall; or seizing on hatred and giving up the body, one may even fall into hell. Hell, with its iron beds and copper pillars and all its cruel retributions, is established precisely out of compassion for living beings. All these are dwelling in marks. If one gives up one's life holding a nihilistic view, as in the passive sort who feel the world has nothing to hold to and so do away with themselves, this is dwelling in the marks of non-dharmas, sinking and stagnating in emptiness — better not to renounce at all. Annihilation and sinking into emptiness may also lead to a fall. Therefore in renouncing one should dwell neither in dharmas nor in non-dharmas.

There are also bodhisattvas who give up their lives for living beings; yet if they dwell in the mark of delivering living beings, they too cannot become Buddhas. Therefore the following text of this sutra makes the comparison that giving body and life as many as the sands of the Ganges is not equal to receiving and upholding four lines of verse. Giving body and life as many as the Ganges' sands is something only a bodhisattva can do; an ordinary person does not have so many bodies and lives. Yet it is still not equal to receiving and upholding four lines of verse and speaking them for others, whose merit is greater — because receiving, upholding, reciting, and speaking can bring about Buddhahood.

If cultivation yields no benefit, it is due to no more than two faults: first, failing to grasp the vital point; second, not understanding the principle. If one can grasp the vital point and understand the principle, one will naturally benefit. One must not speak of the nature apart from cultivation, or it is empty talk; one cannot cultivate apart from the nature, or it is blind advance. This sutra speaks of the nature everywhere and contains actual practice everywhere.

Only by arousing the great vow and practicing the great practice can one enter the Buddha's gate. The former section on subduing is the arousing of the great vow; this section on practicing giving is the practice of the great practice. One must practice giving without dwelling anywhere before it is a great practice. With a vow but no practice, the vow is an empty vow; with a vow and with practice, the vow is important and the practice more important still. Without the great vow the great practice cannot arise, and even if practiced it is blind practice. What makes a vow great, what makes a practice great? Only great compassion and great wisdom. 'All the various kinds of living beings, I shall cause them all to enter nirvana without residue and be brought to deliverance' — this is great compassion. 'Thus I deliver measureless, countless, boundless living beings, and yet in truth not one being attains deliverance' — knowing that living beings share one substance, that there is no such thing as a Buddha and no such thing as a living being — this is great wisdom. Only with compassion and wisdom complete can one arouse the great vow and practice the great practice. 'A bodhisattva, with regard to dharmas, should not dwell' — the sickness of ordinary people is clinging everywhere; to be able not to cling is great wisdom. 'Practicing giving' is great compassion. Without compassion the great vow cannot be aroused; without wisdom the great practice cannot be practiced. When compassion, wisdom, vow, and practice are all great, one is a bodhisattva-mahasattva. Only when one is thus complete and perfect is it supreme bodhi. The preceding text, on the great vow, first spoke of great compassion, which is not dwelling in emptiness; for dwelling in emptiness, one cannot arouse the great vow. This text, on the great practice, first speaks of great wisdom, which is not dwelling in existence; for dwelling in existence, one cannot practice the great practice.

Ordinary people can never let go of anything. Why can they not let go? Because there is an 'I' present. The Buddha speaks only of giving, and at the very outset one breaks the 'I.' Advancing a step further, one breaks it in the realm of objects; further still, one breaks it where the mind stirs and moves. The former section spoke of arousing the great mind, yet everywhere it is non-dwelling: this is transforming imperceptibly, dissolving away the view of self. Ordinary people's thought of 'I' is the heaviest; now, for the sake of living beings, one sets the 'I' aside. Whether the utterly stupid egg-born or the exceedingly lofty non-percipient, all must be caused to enter nirvana without residue and be brought to deliverance: this is dissolving the discriminating mind, and it applies the medicine precisely to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. That ordinary people revolve in the six paths and cannot escape is likewise the work of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses; now, by shifting them, it becomes a paramita.

The arousing of the mind must be vast; without vastness one cannot dissolve the view of self. Cultivation, however, must be fine and close. Only after arousing the vast mind can one cultivate the fine and close practice. Therefore one must first contemplate that all living beings are produced by conditions, are fundamentally still, and share one substance; and one must first know how heavy one's own habitual tendencies are and shift them imperceptibly — only then can one cultivate.

Why is the arousing of the great mind spoken of in dependence on subduing the mind? Why is the arising of the great practice spoken of in dependence on not dwelling? This is because, in order to subdue, one should first know where the root of the sickness lies. One should know that living beings become living beings precisely because they have desire, form, and consciousness; hence in the gate of arousing the mind such words are spoken. Working from this point, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses can naturally be transformed. In speaking of fine and close cultivation, it points directly to not dwelling. Hence it can be seen that cultivation must of course be practiced, not dwelt in. Working in this way precisely leaves the sixth and seventh consciousnesses no room to exist, and the true mind naturally reveals itself. This is not dwelling yet dwelling; therefore the following text says, 'should abide as taught.'

The Buddha teaches people: all the various living beings shall be caused to enter nirvana without residue and be brought to deliverance. This is a bodhisattva's arousing of the mind: not yet self-delivered, first delivering others. 'In truth not one being attains deliverance' makes people know that all are produced by conditions, equal and of one substance, and so on. This delivering of others is delivering oneself; it is plainly the simultaneous deliverance of self and others. Yet the Buddha in the end does not speak of delivering oneself, because our clinging to self is heavy, and so he does not speak of it. How are living beings delivered? One must arise in practice. Giving breaks the seventh consciousness's clinging to self and the sixth consciousness's discriminating mind, and this is plainly delivering oneself. Therefore the arousing of the mind must be great: to deliver oneself one must first deliver others, and delivering others is delivering oneself. Coming to cultivation, one first removes the root of one's own sickness; to deliver others one first delivers oneself, and delivering oneself is delivering others. Yet giving on the one hand delivers oneself while in fact delivering others — this is the subtle intent of the Buddha's speaking only of practicing giving.

The ancients said that the line 'one should arouse the mind without dwelling anywhere' can run through the whole sutra. In fact any line can run through it. Take 'not dwelling in marks': it also encompasses non-marks, falls to neither extreme, and practices the middle way — why should it not run through the whole sutra? The wondrousness of Mahayana Buddha Dharma is that one may comprehend it from any side according to one's capacity, and so it is called perfectly fused. Not only do the shallow and the deep see differently according to the person; even the deep see differently again.

The word 'marks' in the preceding text is spoken from the standpoint of the mark of self; the word 'marks' in this text is spoken from the standpoint of dharmas and non-dharmas. In this sutra the later text is often nothing other than a commentary on the earlier. For example, 'should not dwell, practicing giving' is a commentary on the preceding delivering of living beings; 'giving without dwelling in form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas' is a commentary on 'should not dwell'; and 'not dwelling in marks' is again a commentary on giving without dwelling in the six dusts. Some suspect that the Diamond Sutra repeats its meaning from beginning to end; such people do not know how to read the Diamond Sutra. If one understands the relation of later text to earlier text, then not only is there no repetition — one sees that its veins and arteries run through.

In reading this passage of scripture one must again work at contemplation and illumination. The Buddha Dharma never departs from contemplation and illumination, and one must think of it at every moment. One must know that not dwelling in marks is thoroughgoing: from the first beginning of practice all the way to Buddhahood, it is always not dwelling in marks. If in the act of giving one retains a trace of the wish to be thought well of, then imperceptibly one dwells in the six dusts; hence contemplation is indispensable. If one does not retain the wish to be thought well of, but merely feels that one is giving, one dwells in dharmas; hence without contemplation, one dwells without even being aware of it.

Next, contemplate that practicing giving is meant to make us become Buddhas: if one does not contemplate and illuminate, how can one attain it? 'Should give thus' is also a line of Dharma spoken by the Buddha. If, when giving, the mind holds 'should give thus,' that too is dwelling in dharmas. If in every matter we act according to the Buddha's teaching while in the mind there is nothing of the sort, then we do not dwell in the marks of dharmas. If in the mind there is nothing of the sort and yet one still practices with vigor, then we do not dwell in the marks of non-dharmas. 'Should give thus' is still on the outside; 'not dwelling in marks' is the turning inward in pursuit. This is precisely where the work is most pressing. Next, contemplate that not dwelling in marks, though the mind holds nothing of the sort, is still dwelling in marks if this mind is retained. Therefore in contemplation one enters the mind more finely layer by layer: objects and mind, dharmas and non-dharmas, clinging to neither extreme, the double illumination of both extremes. Though the mind grows fine, it is still on the ground of duality, and one must know that while the view of duality is not forgotten, one has not yet been able to transcend the world. All objects in the world are nothing but duality: birth and death, old and young, high and low, long and short, great and small, and so on are nothing but the discriminating mind. Therefore in world-transcending dharmas one must leave the discriminating mind and contemplate on the absolute. Turning the ordinary person's conceptions to the absolute realm is precisely realizing the nature. To realize the nature one must be without thought; 'thought' is the discriminating mind. Where there is a discriminating mind, one falls into duality; falling into duality, one discriminates at every moment and is shrouded by consciousness. One must contemplate until there is no thought before it will do. Yet if the two words 'no thought' still remain in the mind, this is still dwelling in marks. One must reach the point where even the thought of no thought is absent, contemplating closely and densely, before the virtue of the nature can be perfect and bright — only then is it truly not dwelling in marks. The Buddha said that one who can contemplate no-thought is tending toward the Buddha-wisdom. Hence we know that contemplating no-thought is not something one can reach in a moment; one should only advance in this direction, and so it is said to be tending toward the Buddha-wisdom.

Thought is contemplation and contemplation is thought. 'One who can contemplate no-thought,' turned around, means that we should think no-thought. To think no-thought one must use thought, and thought can turn the discriminating mind. The discriminating mind seeks outward; thought seeks inward for the supreme and wondrous realm. When the mind stirs and moves, one removes the discriminating mind, and then according to the Buddha's method thinks inward: this is thinking no-thought. It is the same with Buddha-recitation: when it resonates for a long time, one can be without thought.
(Gui) Second, expounding the reason. Three parts: (Zi) First, questioning and explaining; second, illustrating by simile; third, applying the dharma.
(Zi) First, questioning and explaining.
'Why is this? If a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit is inconceivable.'

To question is to raise up: raising the preceding meaning again and asking and answering oneself. Merit is the double cultivation of merit and wisdom. Merit and wisdom are like the two wheels of a cart and must not lean to either side. Someone says: if the Buddha teaches people not to dwell, why does he again teach people to cultivate merit? This is a mistake. If one does not cultivate merit, then when one has become a bodhisattva or a Buddha and goes to deliver living beings, living beings are stiff and strong and may not be deliverable; hence one must first form affinities with living beings. That is why this sutra everywhere speaks of cultivating merit, while in actual practice it speaks only of giving: it makes one cultivate merit and wisdom together. 'Think' is to peer and surmise; 'measure' is to gauge. It means that it cannot be peered at with the mind's thought, nor gauged with numbers. In giving without dwelling in marks, not dwelling in marks is not dwelling in dharmas, that is, not clinging to existence; giving is not dwelling in non-dharmas, that is, not clinging to emptiness. To give without dwelling in marks and to give while not dwelling in marks — clinging thus to neither extreme — is precisely the Buddha's realm. Therefore the greatness of the merit is inconceivable. This merit refers to becoming a Buddha. The preceding text's arousing of the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is the mind of becoming a Buddha, and it stands exactly opposed to this line. It can be seen that giving without dwelling in marks is the Dharma gate of becoming a Buddha.

The supreme, profound, wondrous Dharma refers to prajna, which is exceedingly deep and exceedingly fine. Hence every line of this sutra is like peeling a banana: not easy to understand. The speaker must gather in the marks and contemplate the mind, and the listener must do likewise. That the scripture everywhere speaks of not dwelling in marks and yet everywhere speaks of merit is precisely the meaning of not falling to either extreme. Not dwelling in marks is not itself inconceivable merit; only giving while not dwelling in marks is inconceivable merit.

The Mahayana Buddha Dharma is spoken as dust and spoken as a moment, spoken horizontally and spoken vertically, perfect on every side. The most essential thing is to break clinging: once there is clinging, one falls to one of the two extremes — if not clinging to existence, then clinging to emptiness — and it is not the middle way. In hearing the Dharma and reading the sutras one must likewise view them from every side. If one clings to one side, one cannot receive the benefit. The Buddha spoke the definitive meaning, not the indefinite. Speaking thoroughly, he still feared the listener would not understand; if he did not speak thoroughly, how could he make people understand? The listener is likewise thus, or the principle of prajna cannot be understood. Hence he spoke from every side. And again, speaking yet not speaking, he left a little for the listener to think over. Had he spoken the exceedingly profound principle out to the last detail, the listener would no longer apply himself. Therefore the Chan patriarchs of old, in instructing students, always left half a line for the person to awaken to himself. Otherwise, to do nothing but copy out lecture notes, without striving in this oneself — what use is a somersault? Look at the preceding text of this sutra: it plainly says to give without dwelling in the six dusts, because dwelling in objects makes the mind impure; one must be entirely without ulterior motive before it will do. Yet here it says merit is inconceivable — is this not a conflict of meaning between the two texts? Is merit not precisely a mark? Why does it everywhere speak of not dwelling, and everywhere speak of merit? One must know that the preceding text teaches people not to dwell in the six dusts, which is to teach people not to cling, and by no means to annihilate the six dusts. The following text's 'with regard to dharmas one does not speak of the mark of annihilation' proves it. In cultivation there are objects: it is not that objects are unwanted, for only by relying on objects can cultivation begin. In giving, to speak of merit is precisely to point out to people the method of beginning. Therefore in teaching people to study the Buddha Dharma, one must rely on objects before one can begin; and in studying the Buddha Dharma oneself, one must likewise rely on objects before one can begin. This sutra says not to dwell in the six dusts, while the Amitabha Sutra describes the six dusts of the Land of Ultimate Bliss throughout — seemingly the opposite, in fact the same, and it precisely shows the loftiness of the Pure Land realm. Suffering living beings, in the stirring of a thought, never leave the six dusts. The wonder of the Pure Land Dharma gate lies in changing the minds of living beings. To contemplate the six dusts of the Land of Ultimate Bliss is not to dwell in emptiness; and thereby to leave the six dusts of the five turbidities is not to dwell in existence. Hence the Buddha Dharma governs the mind not by weight on subduing but by weight on shifting. Causing the minds of living beings to turn toward the six dusts of the Buddha's realm, and so to leave the six dusts of the five turbidities — the method of beginning that clings to neither extreme is just here.
(Zi) Second, illustrating by simile.

'Subhuti, what do you think? Is the space in the east conceivable?' 'No, World-Honored One.' 'Subhuti, is the space in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above and below conceivable?' 'No, World-Honored One.'

As for the word 'no' in 'no, World-Honored One,' the ancient worthies in commenting on the sutras read it as the character fu, for which the dictionaries have no such pronunciation. The reason is that the ancients, in translating sutras, where Sanskrit had no equivalent character, often used an approximate character and gave it another reading to mark the difference — this too was the painstaking care of the translators. For example, wherever the character jie occurs in the various sutras, it is read with the sound xie, so as to show that not only should the words be understood, but one should dissolve back into the self-nature, neither grasping the words nor departing from them, before it will do. Here 'no' is read fu, showing that it is not merely a negation, but carries the sense of a hesitant yes and no. Broadly, where the following text has no explanation, it is taken as a negation; where the following text has an explanation, it is not taken purely as a negation.

'Space is without marks, yet it does not obstruct the unfolding of all marks' — this saying is most worth bearing firmly in mind. The ordinary view takes space to be the absence of everything; that is merely the stubborn emptiness of the Small Vehicle. In fact space encompasses all phenomena; the space spoken of in the Mahayana sutras refers precisely to encompassing all phenomena, and it is because numberless marks are contained within it that the greatness of space is revealed. The emptiness spoken of by the Buddha should always be understood in this way. One must know that to exclude nothing is the emptiness of the supreme meaning — what is called empty yet not empty. To say 'inconceivable' does not mean that being without marks it is inconceivable, but rather that excluding nothing is what makes it inconceivable. To cite the east and then necessarily the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above and below is no idle passage: it precisely shows that any one dharma the Buddha speaks of encompasses the ten directions.

The Buddha's speaking of the Dharma is perfect on every side and cannot be viewed from one side alone. The Avatamsaka, for example, specifically expresses the meaning of layer upon layer without end. For the Buddha's speaking of the Dharma flows forth from the boundless ocean of the nature, and so it is layer upon layer without end. That space is inconceivable, if taken as illustrating merit alone, is still viewing from one side; in fact it illustrates giving without dwelling in marks.

Yet in taking space as a simile the Buddha spoke only of the east, which would already have sufficed for understanding. Why did he again speak of the four directions and above and below? This has five meanings. (1) Any one dharma cited is in its very substance empty, and none should be dwelt in as a mark — even space is so. (2) One should know that east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above and below are all provisional names: facing east, it becomes west; facing south, it becomes north — there is fundamentally no fixed rule. Hence we know that all dharmas are likewise all provisional names, and that no fixed dharma can be obtained; therefore one must not dwell. (3) Since the ten directions are all provisional names, and provisional names are marks, they must not be dwelt in. 'I' and living beings are also provisional names and must likewise not be dwelt in. Yet all dharmas share one substance: in the substance of the nature they are originally one. To understand in this way is to see that mind, Buddha, and living beings are three without difference. Thus the merit is inconceivable; thus giving without dwelling in marks is the Buddha's realm, and how could the greatness of the merit be peered at by ordinary feeling? (4) The ten directions are all within space, and in fact all within a single thought of the mind. Though ten directions are spoken of, they do not obstruct the one space; and though there is one space, it does not obstruct the ten dharma realms. This makes one understand that cause and effect are simultaneous without obstructing the one dharma realm, and that the one dharma realm does not obstruct cause and effect. (5) In citing the ten directions, the principle that space is without marks yet does not obstruct the unfolding of all marks becomes clear of itself. Contemplating from this point, emptiness and existence are simultaneous; and though empty and existent, they are perfectly fused and at ease. Only then can one understand the meaning that giving without dwelling in marks, and the merit of not dwelling in marks, is inconceivable.

That space is taken as a simile and then the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above and below are further cited is no idle passage: it bears on essential meaning and must not be slighted in the least. (1) The ten directions are all within space, which makes one know that the ten dharma realms dwell together in the single thought of every person's mind. (2) Any one direction cited is space, which makes one know that any one dharma cited is in its very substance empty. (3) Since this is so, east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above and below are all merely provisional names, which makes one know that I, person, living beings, and even all dharmas are none of them anything but provisional names. (4) Since they are all provisional names, space is originally one; this makes one know that I, person, living beings, and even the Buddha — all their various differences — are spoken with regard to the marks of provisional names, while with regard to the substance of the nature they are one. Hence it is said: mind, Buddha, and living beings are three without difference; hence it is said to be one dharma realm. One must know that it is because living beings do not penetrate the one dharma realm that, unwittingly and of themselves stirred, they have ignorance. (5) Though there are ten directions, they do not obstruct the one space; though there is one space, it does not obstruct the ten directions. This makes one know that the cause and effect of the ten dharma realms are densely arrayed, yet do not obstruct the one emptiness of nature; and though there is one emptiness of nature, it does not hinder the densely arrayed cause and effect of the ten dharma realms. This is precisely to reveal that space is without marks yet does not obstruct the unfolding of all marks. In this way emptiness and existence are simultaneous, preservation and dissolution are at ease — only then is space inconceivable, and only then is it adequate to illustrate the inconceivability of the merit of giving without dwelling in marks and dwelling in marks while giving. If one spoke of space alone, that would be one-sided emptiness; how could it be the supreme-meaning emptiness of prajna, and what would there be to call the inconceivability of space? The reason space must be spoken of together with the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above and below lies herein, and it should be known in this way. To know it in this way is right knowledge.
(Zi) Third, applying the dharma.
'Subhuti, if a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit is likewise inconceivable.'

The space of the ten directions is without marks yet does not hinder the unfolding of all marks — this is exactly like giving without dwelling in marks. Giving without dwelling in marks is exactly like space being inconceivable. If a bodhisattva can thus have yet not have, be empty yet not empty, then he turns his back on dust and accords with enlightenment. The preceding text says 'giving without dwelling in marks'; here the word 'not' is changed to 'without,' which has deep meaning. For good men and good women who have already aroused the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi possess the capacity for Buddhahood; therefore they are taught to give without dwelling in marks. Here, in teaching the work, one must truly reach the point of being able to be without dwelling, with not a hair's breadth remaining, before it will do.
(Gui) Third, concluding and showing right dwelling.
'Subhuti, a bodhisattva should simply abide as taught.'

The conclusion comes back to non-dwelling being precisely right dwelling; it points straight to 'should not dwell' and again answers 'how should one abide?' The preceding text everywhere spoke of not dwelling and non-dwelling, and here it suddenly says 'abide as taught.' The meaning is that one should abide according to the teaching I have spoken: plainly it is dwelling yet not dwelling, not dwelling yet dwelling, and not annihilation. Weigh the two words 'should simply': it can be seen that apart from abiding in my non-dwelling and non-abiding, there is no other abiding. And it contains the sense of subduing, for subduing is subduing this very dwelling. Again, 'should simply' means that one should abide in the non-abiding of the two extremes as I have taught, and only then is it right dwelling. 'Abide' also has the sense of taking as master: one should simply cultivate according to the non-abiding of the two extremes that I have taught, taking non-dwelling as the master — otherwise it is not Mahayana Buddha Dharma.

These two sections, on arousing the mind apart from marks and on not dwelling in marks, illumine each other. The former speaking of subduing already contains the meaning of not dwelling; this speaking of not dwelling already contains the meaning of subduing. Therefore subduing and non-dwelling are two matters that are one matter. In the beginning of cultivation it is the one word 'renounce.' To be unable to renounce is precisely to cling to the view of self. The Buddha's word 'renounce' is to break the clinging to self. If one can renounce this clinging to self by one part, one breaks one part; breaking it away layer by layer, only at ultimate renunciation is the clinging to self wholly broken. A bodhisattva of equal enlightenment still has one part of clinging to dharmas unbroken; only at the Buddha-fruit is the renunciation ultimate. Hence the Buddha Dharma from beginning to end is but the one word 'renounce.' To renounce is precisely not to dwell in emptiness and not to dwell in existence; it is the mind apart from marks. Only when the mind's measure is vast to the boundless and limitless is it anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; if the mind's measure is narrow and small, how can one renounce? The Buddha does not speak of dwelling: even in Buddhahood one does not dwell in the marks of a Buddha. Hence the Chan patriarchs used the method of the Diamond Sutra entirely, speaking half a line to students without speaking it through, making the student go and think: left is not right, right is not right; the idle thoughts are beaten to shreds, and suddenly it drops away — this is precisely wondrous dwelling.

blocks.text: Seeing the Truth in Accord with Principle, Section Five

inline.s: (Gui) Fourth, further clarifying the why. Two parts: (Zi) First, question, answer, and explanation; second, unfolding the meaning and giving approval. (Zi) First, again two: (Chou) First, the question; second, the answer.
(Chou) First, the question.
'Subhuti, what do you think? Can the Tathagata be seen by means of the body-mark?'

The ancient worthies said: 'With "a bodhisattva should simply abide as taught" the whole Diamond Sutra ceases; its great meaning is exhausted, and what follows is a layer-by-layer severing of doubts.' Severing doubts is certainly so, yet the meaning is still not complete. In the present division into sections, the four words 'further clarifying the why' cost much deliberation. For only when the reason why is unclear do doubts arise; if one knows the reason why, the doubts are severed of themselves.

As for the two words 'body-mark,' the old explanations all take them to mean the transformation body of the thirty-two marks. If so, would not the thirty-two marks in the following text be a repetition? Every word and every line of the Diamond Sutra has deep meaning and there is certainly no repetition. These two words 'body-mark' should be spoken with regard to the living being's own body, and the two words 'Tathagata' refer to the dharma-body inherent in living beings. The preceding text everywhere speaks of not dwelling in marks, and not dwelling is precisely to make one turn marks back to the nature. The mind of living beings is called the Tathagata-garbha, which is to say that living beings inherently possess the dharma-nature; it is only that it is stored away within the self of a person and the self of dharmas. The Buddha teaches not dwelling in marks precisely so that living beings may see for themselves the Tathagata thus stored away. Such an explanation is more intimate. The Buddha's meaning is as if to say: You living beings — can you see your own nature by means of the body-mark?

This section further explains the reason why of the principles spoken above. Of the various principles spoken above, the most essential is the repeated setting forth of not dwelling in marks, and all of it comes back to the one line 'can the Tathagata be seen by means of the body-mark?' The preceding text says that when a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks his merit is inconceivable; the Buddha has explained the reason, but has not yet explained the reason why. For the essential point of not dwelling in marks lies precisely in realizing the nature. All ordinary people, from beginningless time, recognize only a mark; hence they seek outward, turning their backs on enlightenment and joining with dust, and forget their original face. The preceding text speaks of not dwelling in the marks of dharmas and not dwelling in the marks of non-dharmas. 'Dharmas' refers to all things and matters; this stinking bag of skin of ours is what we cling to most among all things and matters. From beginningless time we have clung to it as the body-mark, taking the false as true, not knowing that it is impermanent, arising and perishing. Even one whose views are somewhat loftier knows this body to be illusory, yet still clings to the view that the joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure once aroused are the emotions, and the unmoved state before their arousal is the nature. Such a person thinks that the office of the mind is to think, and that when it thinks it receives something; tracing this to its source and finding nothing to be had, he supposes it is received from Heaven, and so says 'what Heaven decrees is called the nature.'
