The world over, people hold this view, which is wholly different from the Buddha Dharma. What they call the unmoved is precisely what the Buddha Dharma calls a mark. The Buddha's teaching of the unmoved is that whether it be the constant scrutiny and deliberation of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses — on the surface all movement and arising and perishing — the nature is unmoved; even joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure are movement, arising and perishing. If one mistakes the unaroused for the nature, one is sure to be bound by it. In the world, from the sages above to the foolish below, all is this kind of clinging, and it never goes beyond birth and death. Therefore one must recognize this master who is unborn and undying; only then can one avoid being turned by marks, and instead turn marks oneself, not walking along with birth, death, and impermanence — and so one can end birth and death.

The Buddha has people not dwell in marks; the pressing work is here, and the thousand words and ten thousand phrases of the Buddha Dharma say nothing beyond this. This sutra speaks of not dwelling in marks at the very start, precisely to make us recognize this point clearly. To cling to marks is to cling to existence; not to cling to marks is to cling to emptiness — this is the common sickness of all ordinary people. The Small Vehicle is the opposite of ordinary people: understanding that the body-mark is illusory, and that even the unaroused joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure are marks, it realizes one-sided emptiness, ends birth and death, and escapes the three realms. Yet it contracts another sickness, the sickness of clinging to emptiness — and this emptiness is still a mark. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana says that emptiness means emptying out deluded thoughts: one must empty even the unaroused joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure of the stirring mind, and so dwell in no-marks. To think that one-sided emptiness ends birth and death — not knowing that clinging to emptiness is again dwelling in the marks of non-dharmas — is why the Buddha censured it as not according. One must know that where there is a substance there must be a function, and where there is a nature there must be a mark. Formerly, in speaking of the clinging of ordinary people, it was said to be nothing but pursuing marks; one need only know the marks to be false, and that is enough. But if one again clings to emptiness, one falls into annihilation. Nature and mark are not one: nature is nature and mark is mark, substance is substance and function is function; therefore one must not annihilate marks, for to annihilate marks is like a thing having a bottom but no face. Nature and mark are again not different: mark is the manifestation of nature and nature is the root of mark; to have the root but not manifest it is to have substance without function, and therefore the Buddha does not dwell in nirvana. Why? Because living beings are clinging precisely to these marks, and if the Buddha did not manifest these marks he could not deliver them; therefore realizing the substance of the nature is originally for the sake of arising in practice. That the Small Vehicle is censured by the Buddha as a scorched sprout and a rotten seed, fallen into the pit of non-action, is for this reason. This section of text precisely unfolds this principle, so that one may know the reason why the Buddha has people dwell neither in the marks of dharmas nor in the marks of non-dharmas.

The Buddha teaches people to cultivate in order to deliver living beings; if one falls into the pit of non-action, how can one deliver? Therefore prajna's essential point is not dwelling in either extreme: one must not dwell in existence and not dwell in emptiness before one can accord with the nature. Again, the nature is without marks and yet not without marks. Because it is without marks, one must not cling to existence and must not dwell in dharmas. Because it is not without marks, one must not cling to emptiness and must not dwell in non-dharmas. Precisely because the nature is without marks and yet not without marks, ordinary people cling to the one side of existence and cannot see the nature, and the Small Vehicle clings to the one side of nothingness and likewise cannot see the nature. The thousand sutras and ten thousand treatises say nothing but this principle, and the commentaries of the great masters unfold nothing but this principle.

Therefore the 'body-mark' here should not be spoken with regard to the Buddha's body, but must be spoken with regard to the body-mark of living beings themselves. From the Buddha above to all living beings below, all possess this mark. The Buddha realized the dharma-body, and so is called the Tathagata; and all living beings, in their joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure and the stirring of their minds, are fundamentally unawakened. Yet what can become a Buddha is precisely this mind of living beings. Hence this mind is the Tathagata; it is only obscured by ignorance, and so is named the Tathagata-garbha. The Buddha's asking this is to test Subhuti and the assembly, and even living beings of the future: how, after all, can the not dwelling in marks that I have spoken above allow one to see the nature in marks? If one answered that the Tathagata can be seen, one would be dwelling in the marks of dharmas, an ordinary person. If one answered that the Tathagata cannot be seen, one would be dwelling in the marks of non-dharmas, of the Small Vehicle.
(Chou) Second, the answer. Again two: (Yin) First, the double clarification; second, the explanation accomplished.
(Yin) First, the double clarification.
'No, World-Honored One. One cannot see the Tathagata by means of the body-mark.'

Readers of the Diamond Sutra have always read 'one cannot see the Tathagata by means of the body-mark' as one sentence. Miaoxu has recited and upheld this sutra for more than forty years, and some ten-odd years ago happened to realize that it should be read as two sentences, though he still dared not decide. Later, reading Master Nanyue's lecture on the Lotus Sutra — 'only a Buddha together with a Buddha can exhaust the real mark of all dharmas: what is called the suchlike mark of dharmas, the suchlike nature, the suchlike substance, the suchlike power, the suchlike action, the suchlike cause, the suchlike condition, the suchlike fruit, the suchlike reward, the suchlike beginning, end, and ultimate equality' — which has three ways of dividing the sentences, he then dared to decide on two sentences. But this sort of method can be used only with the sutras of the emptiness school and with the sutras translated by Master Kumarajiva.

The old explanations hold that the body-mark is of course empty: spoken from the dharma-body, the transformation body too is an illusory mark, and so it is said that the Tathagata cannot be seen. Yet the meaning is not exhausted; by such an explanation one would be dwelling in the marks of non-dharmas. One must know that the 'no' in 'No, World-Honored One' is a hesitant yes and no, and cannot be taken wholly as a negation. Since he answers 'cannot' and yet says 'can,' it is a double clarification. Moreover, if it were entirely a negation, why should the next line add the word 'see'? Subhuti's meaning is that one cannot take the mark as the nature and see the Tathagata by means of the body-mark; yet the mark is manifested from the nature, and so one can also see the Tathagata by means of the body-mark. Hence the following text again declares 'the body-mark as spoken of by the Tathagata.'

Read as one sentence, it makes no sense in fact, in principle, or in wording. If one answered thus, that the Tathagata cannot be seen by means of the body-mark, then Subhuti would have awakened only to the point that marks are marks and the nature is the nature — still a Small Vehicle view, fallen into one-sided emptiness, not the supreme-meaning emptiness; how could he be called foremost in understanding emptiness? Moreover, in the preceding eight assemblies it was always Subhuti who was the interlocutor, and he had even spoken on the World-Honored One's behalf of the principle of clinging to neither extreme. How could he here, on the contrary, fail to understand? This does not accord with the facts. In the opening sequence of this sutra, the World-Honored One, in dressing and eating, displayed the great emptiness samadhi. The crowd did not know it, but Subhuti had already grasped its principle, and as soon as he opened his mouth he praised the World-Honored One as rare: 'the Tathagata is good at protecting and remembering the bodhisattvas, good at entrusting the bodhisattvas.' Plainly he saw the Tathagata manifesting the marks of an ordinary person, and saw that marks do not obstruct the nature. How could it be that after the World-Honored One's two rounds of instruction he still saw only one side, with nature and mark unreconciled? Then the word 'rare' in the preceding text would have no ground, and the two phrases 'the Tathagata is good at protecting and remembering' would be utterly meaningless. This does not accord with principle. Again, read in this way, it would be entirely a negation, and the one line 'No, World-Honored One' would suffice; why add 'see the Tathagata by means of the body-mark,' and why add the word 'see'? This does not accord with the wording.
(Yin) Second, the explanation accomplished.
'Why is this? The body-mark as spoken of by the Tathagata is not the body-mark.'

That the body-mark as spoken of by the Tathagata is not the body-mark is the double illumination of both extremes. The nature is the substance of the mark, and the mark is the function of the nature. The mark cannot be fused without the nature, and the nature cannot be revealed without the mark. Apart from the mark there is no nature to speak of, and apart from the nature there is no mark to speak of. It is only a matter of whether one clings or not. One who clings to marks finds that the mark becomes an obstruction and he cannot see the nature; therefore the answer is 'cannot.' If one does not cling, then in the mark one can see the nature. A mark is like the surface of a thing and the nature like its interior: if the surface of a thing is clear as glass, one can see its interior. Hence the answer is that the Tathagata can be seen by means of the body-mark. For not clinging is not falling to either extreme, and one need not, like the Small Vehicle, annihilate form to reveal emptiness and annihilate marks to see the nature — which is the following text's 'one does not speak of the mark of annihilation.' The whole principle of prajna lies herein, and one must contemplate and illuminate it and work at it carefully.

With regard to the mark, one speaks of the body-mark; with regard to the nature, one speaks of the very substance being empty, the nature being fundamentally without marks. With regard to the mark, one says that mark is mark and nature is nature, that the mark is false and the nature is real — hence 'cannot.' With regard to the nature, one says that the mark is originally empty in its very substance and that the nature can fuse the mark, so that the principle of the real is at once revealed; why then must one leave the false mark to see the real nature? Hence 'can see the Tathagata.' Only such an explanation accords with Subhuti's role as interlocutor in requesting the Dharma. The crowd, seeing the Buddha dress and eat and manifest the marks of an ordinary person, clung to the marks of an ordinary person and did not see the Tathagata. Subhuti saw the nature through the mark and, knowing the Buddha's not dwelling in marks, saw the Tathagata. Hence this is precisely the accomplished explanation of the double clarification.
(Zi) Second, unfolding the meaning and giving approval. Two parts: (Chou) First, clarifying that the nature is fundamentally not mark; second, clarifying that seeing the mark is seeing the nature.
(Chou) First, clarifying that the nature is fundamentally not mark.
The Buddha told Subhuti: 'All marks whatsoever are false.'

The compiler of the sutra placed 'the Buddha told Subhuti' here to show that the following principle is important. This line is the approval; what follows expands it further. The question and answer just now spoke only of the body-mark; in fact all marks whatsoever are false. That you said 'cannot' is very true, for the nature is fundamentally not mark. This word 'false' is broad in meaning: false means unreal. Knowing it to be unreal, one should turn the light back and shine within, and must not seek outward among marks, but return quickly to the nature. The nature is fundamentally real: how can one see the real by means of the unreal? Knowing this, the sickness of ordinary people can be avoided, and one does not fall into rebirth.
(Chou) Second, clarifying that seeing the mark is seeing the nature.
'If one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata.'

'All marks' means all marks, that is, all marks whatsoever. One need only understand thoroughly that all marks are false; then one does not pursue the false and knows there is the real. Hence, seeing all marks as non-marks, the mark cannot obstruct the nature, and one sees the Tathagata. Why annihilate marks? In the mark itself one can see the nature. That you answered 'one can see the Tathagata' is entirely right. The word 'see' also involves work: one must truly be able to see all marks as non-marks before it will do. If one merely speaks of the principle, one cannot see the Tathagata. As for the word 'then,' the circulating editions have always had 'namely'; here it follows the Tang manuscript, which has 'then.' 'Then' and 'namely' are interchangeable in general, but it can be understood as 'forthwith' and not as 'just so.'

All marks whatsoever, being false, should none of them be dwelt in. Therefore the preceding teaching of the marks of dharmas and the marks of non-dharmas already includes all marks; and the Buddha's teaching of not dwelling in marks is precisely to make one see the Tathagata. If one clings to the transformation body, one cannot see the dharma-body. Hence not dwelling in marks is precisely to make one see the nature. Again, not dwelling in marks is not clinging; not clinging, one is not turned by marks, and moreover marks are turned by oneself. Therefore one need only understand thoroughly that they are false; one need not annihilate them, nor may one annihilate them, for marks are originally manifested from the nature. The Buddha has people neither cling to worldly dharmas nor loathe them. Ordinary people cling to marks, dwelling in the marks of dharmas and giving rise to affliction; practitioners loathe worldly dharmas, again dwelling in the marks of non-dharmas and giving rise to affliction. One must know that the nature is fundamentally without marks and yet not without marks, and cannot be annihilated. In our work we must first contemplate and illuminate; after a long time we can dwell in illumination, and at the last can see through illumination. Cultivating according to the Buddha's teaching of clinging to neither extreme, practicing on and on until the work is ripe and deep beyond deep, only then is it prajna-paramita, and only then does one truly see all marks as non-marks — which is the Heart Sutra's 'seeing through illumination that the five aggregates are all empty, and so passing beyond all suffering and distress.' The Heart Sutra's 'form' is this sutra's 'mark'; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure and the stirring of the mind. Only when one has illuminated them all to be empty is it 'all marks as non-marks.' 'All empty' means the three emptinesses, not the mere emptiness of the Small Vehicle. Therefore it further says, 'form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form.' Since thus spoken, form and emptiness are still two separate pieces; therefore it further says, 'form is precisely emptiness, emptiness is precisely form.' This is emptiness and existence at the same time, and it accords with the four lines 'all marks whatsoever are false.' 'All marks whatsoever are false' accords with 'emptiness is precisely form,' for all provisional names are in their very substance empty. 'If one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata' accords with 'form is precisely emptiness': form being emptiness, it can be seen that emptiness is not outside form, and why annihilate form to reveal emptiness? Hence it says, 'then one sees the Tathagata.' To see the Tathagata is to see the nature. Not clinging to marks, one can pass beyond all suffering and distress.

Suffering and distress are measureless; to name the greatest: the fragmentary birth and death of ordinary people, and the transformation birth and death of the Small Vehicle. An ordinary person's body has long and short, his life has longevity and early death, and he flows through birth and death — this is called fragmentary birth and death. The Small Vehicle realizes that the nature is without marks; having attained the substance, it could manifest marks, but it fears suffering and will not enter the world to deliver living beings, and subtle arising and perishing stirs in its mind — the Buddha names this transformation birth and death. If one sees the Tathagata, one can pass beyond such suffering and distress. Passing beyond suffering and distress comes from seeing the Tathagata, and seeing the Tathagata comes from seeing through illumination; therefore in one's work the most essential thing is contemplation. If one dissolves this passage of scripture back into the self-nature, then when meeting any mark, the first step of the work is to contemplate that all marks whatsoever are false; and as for form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas, one contemplates all marks as non-marks.

Someone may doubt that amid the toil of the dust it is not easy to contemplate. Let us take Shanghai as an example. What we hear all day long is the sound of carts, the sound of people, and all sorts of clamorous sound. One must know that such sounds arise and perish without cease; and these living beings who come and go in crowds are all busy with food and clothing, not their own masters. Yet in fact these are not the sounds of carts, of people, or of clamor: they are the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and no-self, empty in their very substance. Yet they are plainly sounds — and to contemplate thus is to cling neither to existence nor to emptiness; it is the sound of prajna-paramita. Therefore whatever line of the scripture it may be, all can be contemplated. Walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, never apart from this, one's benefit is inexhaustible. Thus, in relying on the words to arouse contemplation and illumination, one must first go and read the sutra: this is the sutra turning me. As for contemplation, that is me turning the sutra. When the sutra turns me, the sutra shifts my ordinary feeling; when I turn the sutra, that is the more important work. This passage of scripture explains the reason why of the preceding text, and is the summary conclusion of subduing the mind, not dwelling, and the rest. Hence to contemplate according to this text is no different from contemplating the preceding text.

'All marks whatsoever are false; if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata.' To see the Tathagata is to see the nature; seeing the nature is the reason why of not dwelling in marks. To see the nature by one part is to be a bodhisattva of the first ground, no longer retreating from the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; to see it to the ultimate is to become a Buddha, which is the reason why of the preceding text's inconceivable merit. When one becomes a Buddha and sees the nature, the dharma-body is manifested, filling space throughout; this is the reason why of the preceding text's use of space as a simile. One must know that this sutra, from first to last, speaks throughout of non-dwelling. The preceding text's not dwelling in marks is the explanation of 'should not dwell.' Therefore, as soon as he opens his mouth, he first speaks of subduing the mind: 'all the various kinds of living beings, I shall cause them all to enter nirvana without residue and be brought to deliverance' — this teaches us not to dwell. Delivering measureless living beings to Buddhahood points out to us the Dharma gate for arousing the mind; 'in truth not one being attains deliverance' then sweeps away even this dharma, and this points out to us not dwelling in the marks of dharmas. Afterward it says that a bodhisattva should not dwell, again teaching people not to dwell in the marks of dharmas; and 'practicing giving' teaches people not to dwell in the marks of non-dharmas. Though it then says 'should simply abide as taught,' the meaning is still to teach people to abide in non-dwelling. This is the ancient worthies' saying: only seek the stilling of delusion, and do not go further seeking the real. The real is the true mind, which is also suchness; 'should' means such and equal. Why such and equal? Because the substance of the nature is so of itself. Having this substance of the nature, one can manifest marks. Therefore one who has realized it must not retain this true mind; for once one seeks the real, that is the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, and it becomes delusion. The ancient worthies called this 'clinging to difference': clinging to difference is to divide the real and the false into two, which is not equality. Hence it is said, 'should abide as I have taught,' in order to subdue the deluded mind. Ordinary people are all deluded mind; only when the deluded mind is removed part by part does the true mind appear part by part. 'Only seek the stilling of delusion, and do not go further seeking the real' — this is the meaning.

'All marks whatsoever are false': as soon as one dwells, it is false. Therefore the preceding text, at its opening, speaks of subduing and not of dwelling. Why then does it again say, 'if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata'? This speaks of the benefit of non-dwelling. If one can see all marks as non-marks, one sees the true nature. This is the summary conclusion of the preceding text's not speaking of dwelling but of subduing, and of 'should simply abide as taught.' From this it can be known that the Diamond Sutra's writing moves like a heavenly steed across the sky, while its exposition of principle is as fine as a needle and as dense as thread, opening everywhere and concluding everywhere. In reading this passage, it is like a strange peak suddenly rising, seemingly unconnected with the preceding text; in fact it is the summary conclusion of the preceding. It is just like layered mountains and folded waters, wrapped layer upon layer, with the coming of the dragon and the going of its veins everywhere, and a concluding hollow everywhere. As for the wording, it speaks on one side and sweeps away on the other, which is precisely not dwelling in the marks of dharmas and not dwelling in the marks of non-dharmas — truly worthy to be called the prajna of words. In reading and lecturing on this sutra, in the earlier text one must draw in the later text, and in the later text one should look back to the earlier. For example, 'all marks whatsoever are false' corresponds to the later four lines, 'if one seeks me by form, or seeks me by sound.' And 'if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata' is in constant communication with the later 'with regard to dharmas one does not speak of the mark of annihilation.'
The section 'further clarifying the why' has four essential meanings.

(1) The preceding text used only space to illustrate inconceivable merit, explaining the reason why one should give without dwelling in marks. Here it further clarifies that if one does not dwell in marks, one can see the Tathagata's substance of the nature — this is the reason why that merit is inconceivable as space.

(2) The preceding text spoke of not dwelling in marks, guarding against those who do not understand suspecting it to mean annihilating marks. Here it further clarifies that it is not grasping, and by no means annihilating the marks: this is the saying 'if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata.' This is the reason why of not dwelling in marks.

(3) The preceding text spoke of the causal practice, which should not dwell in marks, guarding against the doubt that not only do all living beings have the body-marks of the four elements and five aggregates of suffering fruit, but even the World-Honored One's ultimate fruit manifests the body-mark of sixteen or eight feet and thirty-two marks — how can one not dwell? (The ancients cited only the body-mark of the Tathagata's fruit-virtue; I hold that it can also apply to all living beings, which is more complete in meaning, since the following text plainly says 'all marks whatsoever.' And further on there is the question whether the Tathagata can be seen by the thirty-two marks, which refers specifically to the fruit-virtue.) Here it clarifies that none of them may be dwelt in. With regard to the fruit-virtue, to dwell is to be unable to see the Tathagata; with regard to the suffering fruit, to dwell is to be unable to see the inherently possessed Tathagata-garbha. This is the reason why of 'should simply abide as taught,' that is, of 'should not dwell in marks.'

(4) The Small Vehicle does not fuse nature and mark: it takes sound and form as the Buddha, while in its own cultivation it falls into clinging to non-action. Here it clarifies that in making offerings to the Buddha one must not cling to form-marks and so see the Tathagata, and that in one's own cultivation one should not be empty either, but only not cling to marks; then form is precisely emptiness and mark is precisely nature, with nature and mark perfectly fused and unobstructed and at ease. This is precisely the reason why the World-Honored One spoke the prajna Dharma to cause them to turn from the small toward the great.

blocks.text: Genuine Faith Is Rare, Section Six

inline.s: (Xin) Second, the arising of faith. Four parts: (Ren) First, selecting and showing the faculties; second, clarifying the merit; third, concluding and revealing the middle way; fourth, questioning, explaining, proving, and accomplishing. (Ren) First, again two: (Gui) First, the question; second, the answer.
(Gui) First, the question.
Subhuti said to the Buddha: 'World-Honored One, are there living beings who, hearing such words and chapter-and-verse, give rise to true faith?'

Wherever this sutra places 'Subhuti said to the Buddha,' it is to treat the matter with gravity, because what is said is the most essential principle. 'Are there' means 'are there many?' 'Such' refers to the preceding section that directly showed. 'Words' means the Dharma spoken above. 'Chapter-and-verse' does not mean a single chapter or a single line: Master Kumarajiva followed the idiom of this land, for the explanations of the Chinese in expounding the classics were mostly called chapter-and-verse. These two words refer to the principle spoken above. 'True faith' is not an idle and vague faith; it is the ability to understand the true meaning of such words and chapter-and-verse. Subhuti's question here puts weight on true faith, that is, on showing us that with regard to such words and chapter-and-verse one must give rise to true faith before it will do. What the World-Honored One has spoken above is exceedingly deep; all living beings who hear it will of course give rise to faith. Yet are those who can give rise to true faith many or not? I fear they are not many. For the principle being so deep, to give rise to true faith is impossible without the sharpest faculties and keenest wisdom, and such faculties are not often seen. After all, must they be of the sharpest faculties and keenest wisdom, or need they not be?
(Gui) Second, the answer. Again two: (Zi) First, selecting the faculties capable of faith; second, showing the thickness of former roots.
(Zi) First, selecting the faculties capable of faith.

The Buddha told Subhuti: 'Do not speak thus. After the Tathagata's extinction, in the last five hundred years, there will be those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit, and toward these chapter-and-verse passages they can give rise to faith and take them as true.'

The compiler of the sutra placed 'the Buddha told Subhuti' here to show that what is said is important. The phrase 'do not speak thus' is the World-Honored One directly stopping Subhuti's mouth, so that he may not speak in this way. Not only can the present assembly give rise to true faith; even after the Tathagata's deliverance, down to the last five hundred years, there will be those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit, and toward these chapter-and-verse passages they can give rise to faith. That they can give rise to faith is to take these chapter-and-verse passages as the true meaning. Only these two kinds of people, those who keep the precepts and those who cultivate merit, can give rise to faith toward these passages; others cannot. The word 'these' also refers to the words and chapter-and-verse. 'As true' means being able to understand the principle of this sutra. In working from this point, the ability to give rise to faith depends wholly on taking it as true. Many great men of letters in ages past read the Tripitaka more than once, yet when asked about their practice, there was none at all: this is the sickness of not taking it as true. To take it as true is the direct answer to Subhuti's question whether true faith arises.

Subhuti's question is, on the one hand, to make people give rise to true faith, and on the other, a concern that so profound a principle cannot be truly believed without great faculties; his intent is also sound. Why did the Buddha stop his mouth? This contains three essential meanings, as can be seen from the following text. (1) One must not slight living beings: in the last five hundred years there will still be such people, how much more so now. (2) One must not obstruct others' good thoughts and cause them to grow discouraged, as can be seen from the following text's 'planting all good roots at the places of measureless thousands of ten million Buddhas.' (3) There is no need for the sharpest faculties and keenest wisdom: only the two kinds of people who keep the precepts and cultivate merit can give rise to faith. The first two meanings arise from the third. For these two kinds of people, who keep the precepts and cultivate merit, are not seen to be of high wisdom; and those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit seek blessings, and with regard to the exceedingly profound Dharma gate originally have the mind to shrink back. Therefore the Buddha warned him not to speak thus.
